name: Design a Feature Flag and Experimentation Platform
intent: Let engineers turn features on for chosen users and percentages without deploying, evaluate every flag in microseconds with no network call, switch a broken feature off everywhere within seconds, and measure whether a change helped.
codeTitle: a flag SDK with sticky bucketing and a cached ruleset
finalIntro: One rollout change, from review to a user's first request and the experiment result.
prompt: Design a feature flag platform for a company with 500 engineers, 200 services and 20,000 server instances, plus web and mobile apps. Teams create flags, target users by attribute and percentage, roll a feature out gradually, kill it instantly if it misbehaves, and run experiments that compare a new behavior with the old one. A flag check sits on the request path of every service, so it must be fast and must keep working when the flag service is down.
functional: Define flags with a default value, targeting rules (by user attribute or segment) and a percentage rollout
Evaluate a flag for a user inside the application, with the same answer every time for the same user
Change a flag without a deploy, with a kill switch that works in seconds
Review and approve changes to production flags, and keep an audit log of who changed what
Record which variation each user saw (exposure) and compute experiment metrics from it
Find flags that are no longer needed and help remove them
nonFunctional: A flag check takes microseconds and makes no network call
An ordinary change reaches every instance in about 10 seconds, and a kill switch in 2 seconds
A flag service outage must not break any application, so checks keep working from the last known rules
A user keeps their variation when the rollout percentage rises, and never sees it flip back
Tens of thousands of instances without overloading the flag service
Every production change is attributable, reversible and reviewed

firstAttempt.text: One table of flags in a database. Every time the code checks a flag, it calls the flag service, which reads the row and, for a percentage rollout, picks a random number. Admins edit the rows in a simple page.
limits: A network call on every check adds a round trip to every request, and the flag service becomes a dependency of everything
If the flag service or its database is down, every flag check fails and so does every service
Millions of checks per second land on one service
A random number per check means the same user sees the feature on one request and off the next
Anyone can edit a production flag instantly, with no review and no record of who changed it
Nothing records which users saw what, so an experiment can not be measured

nodes.label: Flag table, read on every check

steps.title: Evaluate in the SDK from a cached ruleset, with a stable hash
steps.problem: A network call for every flag check is slow, makes the flag service a dependency of every request, and a random choice per check changes a user's experience from one request to the next.
steps.fix: The flag service sends each SDK the whole ruleset, a small JSON document with every flag, its targeting rules and its rollout percentage. The SDK keeps it in memory and answers every check locally. A check goes in a fixed order: the kill switch first, then the targeting rules (for example plan equals internal), then the percentage rollout. For the percentage, the SDK hashes the flag's salt together with the user id and turns the hash into a number from 0 to 9,999. The user is in if that number is below the rollout, so 30% means below 3,000. The hash is deterministic, so a user always gets the same answer for a flag, on every instance and every request.
steps.tradeoff: A check costs microseconds, the flag service is off the hot path, and results are stable. Every SDK holds a copy of the rules, so copies can differ for a moment, and rules that contain private user lists can not be sent to a browser, which is why client-side SDKs ask for the evaluated result instead.

steps.title: Publish the ruleset as a file on a CDN
steps.problem: 20,000 instances polling the flag service every few seconds would be hundreds of requests per second, each possibly carrying a megabyte, and a flag service outage would stop every poll.
steps.fix: Each time a flag changes, the service renders the whole ruleset for the environment into one versioned JSON file and publishes it to a CDN. SDKs poll the CDN URL, usually every 30 seconds with an ETag, so an unchanged ruleset costs a tiny 304 response. The CDN edges refresh from the flag service only when their copy expires, so the service sees a handful of requests per second whatever the size of the fleet. The version number lets an SDK ignore a ruleset older than the one it already has.
steps.tradeoff: The load on the flag service no longer depends on the number of instances, and an outage of the service does not stop reads. A change now takes the cache lifetime plus up to one poll interval to arrive, so with a 30 second cache and a 30 second poll it can take a minute.

steps.title: Stream urgent changes, and survive an outage
steps.problem: Waiting a minute to switch off a feature that is hurting users is too long, and an SDK that starts while the flag service is down has no ruleset at all.
steps.fix: SDKs also keep a Server-Sent Events connection to a stream gateway. When a flag changes, the service pushes a notification and the SDK fetches the new version, so a kill switch reaches the fleet in about two seconds. The poll stays as a fallback in case the stream drops. When the service is down, every SDK keeps serving its last ruleset. An instance that starts with nothing falls back to a ruleset bundled in its image at build time and, failing that, to each flag's coded default, which should be the safe value. After an outage, reconnects are spread with random delays, so the gateway does not meet 20,000 connections in the same second.
steps.tradeoff: Changes arrive in seconds and checks never fail. The fleet needs 20,000 long-lived connections, gateway nodes to hold them, and care about reconnect storms. A bundled ruleset can be weeks old, and a coded default is a guess, so defaults must be chosen with care.

steps.title: Review changes, keep an audit log, and allow rollback
steps.problem: A flag edit changes production behavior as surely as a deploy does, yet it takes effect at once and nobody can tell who flipped what.
steps.fix: Changes go through an approval workflow. In a production environment, a change request needs approval from the flag's owning team before the workflow applies it, with rules such as a larger rollout step needing a second reviewer. The kill switch has a fast path that needs no approval, because it only turns things off. Every applied change is appended to an audit log with the user, the time, the reason and the before and after values, and each change produces a new numbered ruleset version, so going back is publishing an older version. Credentials are separate for each environment, and SDK keys can only read rulesets.
steps.tradeoff: Production changes are accountable and reversible, and an incident can start with the question of what changed. Approvals slow routine changes, so teams need sensible rules (for example no approval in a test environment) or they will route around the process.

steps.title: Record exposures and compute experiment results
steps.problem: A rollout says who could see a feature, and an experiment must know who actually saw each variation, and what they did next.
steps.fix: When code evaluates a flag that is part of an experiment, the SDK queues an exposure event with the user, the flag, the variation and the ruleset version. It sends the events in batches, drops repeats for the same user and flag, and may sample. The events go through a queue into an event store, where they are joined with product events such as purchases. The analysis compares the variations on each metric, checks that the split is close to what was configured, and shows confidence intervals. Because bucketing is a stable hash, each user stays in one variation for the whole experiment.
steps.tradeoff: Teams get a measurement instead of a feeling, and the exposure record is the basis for debugging. Events add traffic and storage, a user is counted only if the check really ran, and a split that drifts from the plan (a sample ratio mismatch) means the data should not be trusted.

steps.title: Find stale flags and clean them up
steps.problem: Flags that stay forever become dead branches, hidden dependencies and a growing ruleset, and nobody remembers what is safe to delete.
steps.fix: Every flag has an owner, a type (release, experiment, permission or operational) and, for temporary types, an expected end date. A cleanup job joins the flag store with the evaluation and exposure data: flags that have served a single value to everyone for several weeks, or that were never evaluated, are marked stale. The owner is notified and gets a link to the places in the code that reference the flag, and ideally an automatic pull request that removes the losing branch. Permanent flags, such as a kill switch, are marked so they are not flagged.
steps.tradeoff: The codebase and ruleset stay small, and old branches stop hiding bugs. It needs ownership data to be kept up to date, and tooling to find usages in code, and it creates work for teams that would rather ship features.

failures.scenario: The flag service or the CDN is down
failures.impact: SDKs can not fetch new rules, so changes (including a kill switch) do not arrive, and new instances have nothing to start from.
failures.answer: Running instances keep their last ruleset and keep answering checks, so no application fails. Instances that start with no ruleset use the bundled one, then the coded default, and keep retrying with backoff and random delays. Kill switches are therefore best placed in a fast path that the stream and the CDN both carry, and the application should have its own circuit breaker for risky dependencies.

failures.scenario: A bad rule is published and checkout starts failing
failures.impact: A change that was approved but is wrong affects every instance within seconds.
failures.answer: The kill switch turns the flag off in about two seconds, or the previous ruleset version is published again. Dashboards tie error rates to flag changes so the cause is found quickly, the audit log shows the exact change, and large rollouts go in steps (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) with a watch on the metrics between them.

failures.scenario: 20,000 streams reconnect at the same moment
failures.impact: After a gateway restart or an outage, every SDK reconnects and downloads the ruleset at once, which overloads the service that just recovered.
failures.answer: Reconnects use exponential backoff with random jitter, so they spread over many seconds. The ruleset is fetched from the CDN, not from the service, and the gateway sheds connections it can not serve while the SDKs keep their cached rules.

failures.scenario: Someone changes the salt of a running experiment
failures.impact: Every user is re-bucketed, so users switch variation in the middle, the groups are polluted and the result is meaningless.
failures.answer: The salt is set once when the flag is created and the console does not allow editing it. A rollout that only raises the percentage keeps all users already in. An exposure check compares the observed split with the configured one and flags a sample ratio mismatch.

failures.scenario: A user sees the new feature on one server and not on another
failures.impact: While a change spreads, two instances hold different versions, so the same user can be shown the feature on one request and not on the next.
failures.answer: The stream and a short poll interval shorten the window to seconds. For flows where it matters, such as a multi-step checkout, the first decision is saved in the session, or the service that owns the flow decides once and passes the result along. Exposure events carry the ruleset version, so analysis can tell the instances apart.

alternatives.title: Where the flag is evaluated

options.name: In the SDK, from a cached ruleset
options.pro: Microseconds, no network, works during an outage
options.con: Every instance holds all the rules, so private user lists can not be shipped to browsers

options.name: Remote call to an evaluation service
options.pro: Rules stay private, and one place to change
options.con: A round trip and a dependency on every check

options.name: At the CDN edge
options.pro: Close to browsers and mobile apps, with rules kept off the device
options.con: Evaluation logic must run in the edge runtime, and context is limited

alternatives.pick: Local evaluation for server SDKs, and an edge or server evaluation that returns only the evaluated flags to browsers and mobile apps.

alternatives.title: How changes reach the SDKs

options.name: Polling
options.pro: Simple, works through any proxy, and the load is predictable
options.con: Staleness up to the interval, and shorter intervals cost more requests

options.name: Streaming (SSE)
options.pro: Changes arrive in about a second
options.con: Long-lived connections, gateway capacity, and reconnect storms

options.name: CDN-cached ruleset
options.pro: Cheap and scales to any fleet
options.con: Adds the cache lifetime to the delay of a change

alternatives.pick: A CDN-served ruleset for scale, polled as a baseline, with a stream on top for fast changes such as a kill switch.

alternatives.title: How a user gets a variation

options.name: Hash of the user id and the flag salt
options.pro: Stable without storing anything, the same on every instance, and a higher percentage keeps everyone already in
options.con: Changing the salt reshuffles everyone, and the split is only close to the target for large groups

options.name: Random on every check
options.con: A user flips between variations and experiments are meaningless

options.name: Stored assignment per user
options.pro: Exact control, and users can be moved by hand
options.con: A lookup on the hot path and a table with a row for every user and flag

alternatives.pick: A hash of the user id and the flag salt, with stored assignments only for the few cases that need to be pinned.

alternatives.title: What to do when no ruleset is available

options.name: Fail closed: the flag is off
options.con: Turns off features that are live for everyone, and can break a page that expects the new behavior

options.name: Fail open: the flag is on
options.con: Shows unfinished features, and undoes a kill switch

options.name: A ruleset bundled at build time, then a coded default
options.pro: Mostly right, with the safe value as the last resort
options.con: Can be old, and needs a build step

alternatives.pick: The bundled ruleset first, then a default chosen per flag: off for new features, on for flags that guard long-lived behavior.
